items.excerpt: In this latest instalment of the Secret History of Film Music, Philip Brophy considers how Jon Brion’s music engenders sympathy for the flawed characters in Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025) and Punch-Drunk Love (2002), and Greta Gerwig’s Lady Bird (2017). items.body: In this latest instalment of the Secret History of Film Music, Philip Brophy considers how Jon Brion’s music engenders sympathy for the flawed characters in Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025) and Punch-Drunk Love (2002), and Greta Gerwig’s Lady Bird (2017). As discussed in the previous essay in this series, Jonny Greenwood provides an amazing score for Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025). But two pieces by an earlier composer of Anderson’s films bookend the movie: Jon Brion’s “Bunker Bumper” and “Global Bully”. In One Battle After Another, they function as quietly majestic statements of the drive and exhaustion which propel the intergenerational tale of social reparation and familial separation. “Bunker Bumper” uncoils as a disjointed bossa nova: a gently struck bass drum marks time for the snare, hi-hats and cymbals, skipping with a detached, dainty air. Horns and strings entwine like a billowing flag in slow motion. Sometimes the horns are silenced as the strings climb high, as if they’re searching for something. The music feels absent of harmonic progression; it simply surges, even struggles ahead. It plays near the opening as Pat (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Perfidia (Teyana Taylor) and their radical group French 75 attack a border internment camp. The music intones a sad, fatalistic comment on the limited impact of such revolutionary zeal despite the commitment of its participants. The second track “Global Bully” plays at the film’s end. Years later, Pat relaxes at home with his young adult daughter Willa (Chase Infiniti), offspring of Pat and the long absent Perfidia. The domestic scene shows Willa reading a letter from her mother. In a voiceover, Perfidia acknowledges her mistake in deserting Willa, and expresses hope they will one day meet again. Over a lilting percussive pattern, more strings and horns are orchestrated, but here they coalesce around a chordal pattern. The drums call to mind the tinklers of North American tribal shell shakers engaged in ceremonial dances; the orchestra feels like a calming eulogy played at a church service. The piece acquiesces to how the feisty past can dissolve into a depleted present. It concludes with a touching embrace between Pat and Willa. To label the placement of “Global Bully” here as mere closure misses the weight and precision that Brion’s music bestows on the scene. Across Anderson’s first four films, Brion developed a unique modus operandi of embedding music into movies which, arguably, redefined standard operations of ‘scoring’ and ‘accompaniment’. These two Brion tracks in One Battle After Another were recorded and produced 23 years earlier, for Anderson’s Punch-Drunk Love (2002). That film’s sessions saw Brion continually feeding Anderson with ideas, sketches, recordings and even multitrack breakdowns. All were offered not as thorny strictures, but as flexible flotsam to be experimented with, in terms of how their sono-musical character could enhance and shape onscreen characters. How apt that some of these unused tracks surfaced decades later. As Brion has said: “There are lots of [film composers] doing great things, but it comes down to the director’s ‘follow-through’.” A small suite of prepared piano and percussion ensemble pieces makes up a sizable part of the Punch-Drunk Love score. They sound jittery and clackety, like a wooden digestive system attempting to process parts of a drum kit. They initially read as sound effects more than music – a perceptual doubting, enabled by Gary Rydstrom’s deft mix which folds Brion’s trap kit into Christopher Scarabosio’s sound design (who has handled every Paul Thomas Anderson film since). “Le Petit Chateau” and “Hands And Feet” were based on micro-cassette recordings Brion made of Anderson verbally articulating his ideas for rhythms he wanted to use as timing devices for the film’s long tracking shots. The voice of Anderson became the hands of Brion which became the limbs of Barry (Adam Sandler) who discombobulates throughout the movie in arabesques of anxiety. Upon its release, many assumed the film to be a comedy, thanks to Sandler, but the point was there for an attuned audience: mentally unstable people often appear ‘ridiculous’, but to laugh at their pained performance is inhumane, not to mention imperceptive. Brion’s music plays two roles here. The first, through its percussive moments, is to sonorise the synaptic hell of Barry’s panic attacks, and how desperately out of sync he is with his own body and those around him. The second lies in the sumptuous waltzes (“Punch-Drunk Melody”, “Third Floor Hallway”, “Blossoms & Blood”) which spread the wondrous hope Barry glimpses when he falls in love with Lena (Emily Watson). Irrespective of cliche, the luscious orchestral arrangements welcome the couple into a better, dreamier world. Brion’s music is key in distinguishing Punch-Drunk Love from early 2000s romcom saturation. His arrangements are subtly saccharine, influenced by the lush strings found in rock and pop ballads circa the 1970s, arranged by Van Dyke Parks, Jack Nitzsche and Paul Buckmaster. Their sonority affectionately referenced the easy listening sparkle of 1950/60s hi-fi arrangements by Nelson Riddle and Les Baxter, through to Percy Faith and Paul Mauriat. Brion’s encyclopaedic embrace of recorded popular music is felt in his distinctive melodic sensibility: a transatlantic nexus of solo-Beatles songcraft and Laurel Canyon recording. To be clear, the recording studio rules here, not the concert hall. Punch-Drunk Love used vintage microphones for many of its sessions. The film score brims with detail, space and clarity. Following Punch-Drunk Love, non-mainstream cinema forged a strange meld of nerdy empathy, hipster cynicism and feminist angles in ‘relationship dramedies’: David O Russell’s I Heart Huckabees (2004); Charlie Kaufman’s Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind (2004) and Synecdoche, New York (2008); Miranda July’s The Future (2011); Judd Apatow’s This Is 40 (2012) and Trainwreck (2015); and Greta Gerwig’s Lady Bird (2017). These films cannily merged po-faced ridicule with heartfelt feeling, to varying degrees of success. Yet in all these titles, Brion’s music fortifies their narratives with an endearing romantic sensibility earned by their dysfunctional, antisocial and ‘spectrum’ characters. His Canyon-esque saunter and rich instrumental layering ameliorates any dismissive urges the films’ characters elicit. In Lady Bird, the titular lead (Saoirse Ronan) feels intentionally unlikeable. Equally deliberate is how Brion’s score waltzes around Lady Bird’s teen sense of independence. The film concludes with Lady Bird finally on her own, enrolled in a New York college. At a public phone, she leaves a message for her mother, admitting the rupturing effects of her teen angst created a wedge between them. Brion performs the resonant piano theme like a silent movie accompanist: trilling high notes and copying what’s happening on screen while allowing it space. Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind features similar piano themes played over scenes with onscreen dialogue mixed low. This isn’t simply a formal sonic device: it displaces the viewer/auditor from the psychic space of the story – where you identify or read what’s happening to characters on screen – and relocates you within the characters’ headspace. Positioned this way, the audience can feel a touch exposed, implicated in being present when characters are at their most vulnerable. “Global Bully” fades up in One Battle After Another as we see Lockjaw (Sean Penn) gassed and hear Pat prepare Willa for Perfidia’s letter: death and life fused through emotive exhalation. That seems to be a throughline in the work Brion has provided across the film and music industries. In discussions with Anderson, Brion noted the aim of Punch-Drunk Love was to “feel like a musical, but nobody ever breaks into song”. Brion’s music – and his tremulous voice which has appeared in songs in many of the films mentioned – is similarly shaped by repression, tension and elation, in a fountain of emotional surges. Musical theatre sceptics mostly react against the unbridled emotionalism of onscreen characters liberated from their realistic surroundings. Yet this transcendental effect functions perfectly in recorded songs and popular music in general, generating one of music’s prime private pleasures. Brion and his collaborators have long embraced how song sonics skilfully embedded in the production of a film score can be exhilaratingly transgressive. Wire subscribers can read Philip Brophy’s original Secret History of Film Music columns from the 1990s online in the digital archive. It was revived in 2025 as an online column: previous instalments published on The Wire website can be read here. Wire readers and print and digital subscribers can also find this essay on page 16 of The Wire 512.

items.body: Childhood summers spent in Val D’Arzino made an undeniable impression on Davide Cedolin. The artist describes Friuli in northeast Italy as “Mountain people, feral animals, ancient trees, old crafts, lore, abandoned crashed cars, ghost towns, houses named as boroughs.” On Cjera Aʃìn, the artist performs a feat of alchemy by translating the memory, feeling and sound of the land into a luscious suite. The field recordings are crucial, plunging one into the heart of the remote area; the music fleshes out the narrative. At the very beginning of “Cedolins,” the cricket chorus declares its presence, making Cedolin the accompanist. His guitar work rests in the American Primitive style, warm and wooded, like a hike toward the shady glade portrayed on the cover. As the notes drop down, they do not intimidate; their function is to produce mystery rather than fear. The crickets continue to chirp at the end; this is their territory after all. “Poças,” the first of three long tracks, ups the ante with guest performances on hardy gurdy, shruti box, percussion and double bass. This time the first impression is created by soft rain and the call of a local bird; the piece develops into a thick drone, a mossy blanket of mood, the earth is sending notes through the loam. The players pull back to reveal Cedolin’s banjo, the rain still falling like the accumulation of years, reappearing in the next track with a slightly different timbre, like the memory of a different summer. This time cello colors the mist of memory, producing a wistful, melancholic tone. At some point we hear – or have already heard without recognizing – the artist playing “woods and bones.” The land creates its own music; Cedolin draws from its treasures to make more. The taps in “Cerdevol” could be bones; or the tapping of stones by the creek. The flow receives a generous allotment of time at the end, setting up the crackle of “Benaandants,” an extended work filled with accordion, synth and fire. Val D’Arzino is woven into the artist’s story as the artist’s story is woven into the woods. Echoes and reverberations populate the background of “Cjanâl,” but to the woods, the guitar is the more temporary sound. Warm, gentle narration introduces the final track, which at 12:18 is also the longest. Layer after layer rise to the surface, the artist exposing different facets to the light. In the sixth minute there arrives a softening, with leafy rustles, a slower pace and light percussion that swiftly dissipates to allow the notes to take center stage. The impression is like the region seen from afar, regarded in memory rather than in person, the scratching like notes on paper. In the tenth minute, the music disappears, leaving only scribbles of sound. One cannot pinpoint exactly when the album ends, just as one cannot trace the extent to which a memory can linger in the mind. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Bardic Depths are back with Peter Jones contributing as a full member (one of my favorite collaborations that he's done). This is their fourth studio album release of this decade. 1. "Islands" (8:37) excellent and fresh feeling music based on NeoProg sound palette and stylings. I really like the construct, feel, and flow of this song though it does lag a bit in places. (18.333/20)2. "Fallen Leaves" (3:03) GENESISian 12-string-with-organ and anachronistic melody lines open this as harmonized vocal "doo-doo-doo" lines become woven within the instrumental weave. As this pattern continues--throughout the entire song--I find myself rather surprised--and delighted. It's a really cool and fairly inventive (if �tude-like) piece. (8.875/10)3. "Arribabok" (4:48) borrowing a lot from George Harrison/The Beatles' Indian-influenced soundscapes (which were later further developed by the likes of Daevid Allen with his GONG and other projects as well as Steve Hillage and even Peter Gabriel and David Torn). I love Gareth Gole's Torn-Hillage-like guitar tone and play in the third minute. The vocal and congestion and crescendo at the end of the third minute reminds me of both Peter Gabriel's world music and Karl Jenkins' ADIEMUS music. Nice sax play by Peter in the fourth minute and then a nice d�nouement and return to the original palette in the final minute. (9.125/10)4. "October Sun" (8:12) More excellent vocal-centric NeoProg music that reminds me of the fine fare of both FISH ON FRIDAY and TONY PATTERSON (as well as Dave Longdon-era BIG BIG TRAIN). Though the song construct and instrumental play is rather simple and sedate, the bass and vocal work is quite excellent. I understand how solid, comforting "bedding" of easy-to-digest music can serve as an excellent foundation for the exploration/expression of more sincere ideas above it--and this does happen in this song's second half--and I understand the talent and skill it takes to render such a "bedding"--so I am not as critical of this habit or tendency as I used to be (always looking for the sophistication and instrumental virtuosity in each song). I actually really appreciate the way the band has constructed and rendered this song. (17.75/20)5. "From Empty Trees" (4:41) an instrumental opening that sounds like something Tony Banks would have done for Genesis (or himself?) back in the breakout period of the band's popularity. Gareth's guitar work in his lead time during the third minute is okay but nothing very innovative--and the ascending four-chord motif that follows feels so much like Tom Johnson's "Uncertain Smile" ending jam from his 1983 The The album, Soul Mining (with that amazing piano solo from Jools Holland). (8.75/10)6. "A View" (6:18) a gorgeous NeoGenesis weave of arpeggiating keyboard and acoustic and electric guitars with solid low end support from well-coordinated bass and drums also sees some excellent synth strings orchestra and old Mellotron threads in the weave as Peter sings with his usual folk-bard-like approach. Nice weave of multiple other guitar and keyboard lines topped off by a nice heavily-reverbed sax solo from Peter in the fourth minute which is then followed by a fine electric guitar solo. Peter's voice and vocal styling is so classic, so powerful, so iconic. It's no wonder he's been the vocalist of so many 21st Century NeoProg classics. (8.875/10)7. "Harder to See" (4:09) a little more sophistication, syncopation, and frequent key changing makes this an interesting tune--especially when attending to Peter's vocal (he's got to be spot on for this one!) Once the pattern of the four chord motif is established (almost Van Morrison "Moondance"-like), the music becomes more familiar and, thus, comfortable. The chorus and follow-up d�nouement and fade out come easily but are not quite the finish one might hope for. (8.875/10)8. "Rewind" (9:21) this one opens up as another acoustic guitar- and piano-dominated weave that incorporates a four-way vocal approach, lead and harmonies, reminding me of MOON SAFARI as well as bands like Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young or even Wobbler and The Beach Boys. Nice instrumental work in the instrumental section from the third minute to the fifth and then again after 4:40 when things switch to a more ambient/atmospheric palette. (Who's playing the flutes?) This is very psychedelic in its pastoral dream-like feel--very similar to some of Steve Hackett's best stuff ("Cinema Show," Wind and Wuthering, and his early solo albums). Interesting that the the rest of the song (and album) plays out with this atmospheric instrumental weave--five minutes of it (not unlike that odd prolonged ending to "Dancing with the Moonlight Knight")! Luckily, it's really nice! The boys are obviously serious students of the masterpieces of prog's Golden Age. (18.5/20)Total Time 49:09The band's NeoProg music has continued to develop, progressing into more sophisticated and original realms of prog--that remind me of both Peter Gabriel and Fish On Fridays. With any lineup that includes prog-savant Peter Jones one cannot help but have high expectations. The problem comes with the frequent disappointments that come with the feelings of "underdeveloped," "not fully-realized" or "falling short" of possible potentialities. B+/4.5 stars; an excellent album of creative, top-notch NeoProg from some of England's most reverential and proficient veterans. Highly recommended--especially if you like the NeoProg sub-genre where it might be considered an essential masterpiece.

items.body: Review by Gatot — Hi everyone,.... I'm back after I realize now that my last visit to this site was 2/7/2017 3:31:05 AM EST - 9 years plus ago! Hope everyone is OK and keep on proggin'!I happened to know this new Kamelot album once my old buddy informed me couple of weeks ago and since then I keep playing it and I don't know why I repeat it after I complete the whole tracks here. Yes, I do enjoy the music very much and I have had no idea that Roy Khan left the band and now the lead vocalist is new (maybe couple of years already). Honestly, I cannot differentiate his vocal quality and I tend to say it's very close to Roy Khan.As for this album, I enjoy the opening track that flows nicely to the next one Ashen World (04:13). I enjoy this track and it's actually the main reason I repeat the album again as I want to listen this again. For some reason the flow to the next track Dark Asylum (04:39) happens nicely especially when it reaches Sanctuary (04:25).I have been a great fan of Kamelot since I first listened to their "Karma" album and I always love their music that blends power metal with great melody.Overall, this album is essential and I have been spinning it its entirety more than 10 times already by now. For those of you who love power metal, do not skip this album.Peace on earth and mercy mild!

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — On his Bandcamp page's "liner notes" Tom lists his "Gear used":Fender Rhodes Mk2 (1, 2, 3, 6)Hohner Pianet C (1, 3, 6)Hohner Cembalet I (1, 3, 6)Columbia Elepian (1)Hammond L122 (1, 3, 4, 5, 6)Roland SH2000 (1, 3, 6)SeagullS12 (1, 3, 6)Gibson SG (1, 6)Gibson Les Paul Goldtop (1, 4)Jacobacci LJ612 double neck (1, 2, 3, 6)Fender JazzbassYamaha Rydeen drumkit1. "Didier Dandelion in the Year of the Great Winds" (13:24) sophisticated, more serious Canterbury Style music of the NATIONAL HEALTH sort. A lot of displaying of some mighty fine drumming beneath/within a multi-keyboard vamp. There is a lot of very immersive melodic music here. The multi-instrumentalist seems hell-bent on proving to the world his skills and talents on guitars and keyboards, too. (He is pretty good!) All in all, this is pretty good if sounding a bit like an extension of the 1970s Phil Miller-Dave Stewart-David Sinclair expressions of sophisticated Canterbury Jazz Fusion. The music of this song doesn't always propel--doesn't always feel as if it's moving forward (which was, when I think about it, one of the frequent failings/flaws of the Canterbury artist's music)--but it is an excellent rendering of that era's sound and style. And don't miss the nod to TONY BANKS/Genesis in the "Mad Man Moon" reference in the ninth and tenth minutes as well as the excellent Phil Miller guitar work--which later turns into near-ALLAN HOLDWORTH stuff!--as well as Tom's great drumming. (27.5/30)2. "Mandatory Intermission" (3:47) a piece that feels like a true nod to the most unique genius of the Jazz-Rock Fusion movement: Allan Holdsworth. Even when Tom chooses to settle back into a fuzzy electric guitar over gentle-yet-erudite J-R F band support the lead and music carries with it a kind of reverent "history" of the many stages of growth of the great jazz guitarist: from Bradbury to 'Igginbottom to Nucleus to The Soft Machine up unto the Tempest Jean-Luc Ponty era. Nice homage! (9/10)3. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 1st Movement" (5:21) a Canterbury-inspired weave of bass, drums, electric piano, and guitar that shifts in tempo and dominant (most forward) instrument/sounds between several motifs, including one that introduces a bunch of different keyboard and guitar sounds (including 12-string guitar) while allowing electric bass and drums to remain fairly consistent. I am very much reminded of ANTHONY PHILLIPS and even MIKE RUTHERFORD with a lot of the soundscapes, melodies, and thematic shifts. There's even a little Mike Oldfield in some of the nostalgic melodies and instrumental sound choices, but when Maureen Peircy's "The Northettes'" vocals enter at 4:21 I'm totally taken off guard. Part of me is offended that someone would so blatantly "lift", copy, or replicate such a sacred element of the Canterbury tradition. At the same time, I so welcome and enjoy the brief exposures to the sounds and stylings of these old guys. (9/10)4. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 2nd Movement" (5:35) more Canterbury homage and comfort food. It's as if AI were asked to write some new Dave Stewart (Egg, Khan, Hatfield & The North, National Health) music. It's just too perfect, too much like a re-animation of the old guys: even the production values feel as if I'm listening to some newly-found tapes from 1975 (probably found under the floorboards of the old seaside Wyatt cottage in Lydden [Wellington House]--or better yet--found inside a hash cache inside the walls of Daevid Allen's Bananamoon Observatory in Dei� [Majorca]). I love it while at the same time find myself squirming uncomfortably at the "authentic" feel and sound of the music. I absolutely LOVE hearing more of the peak Canterbury style sound palette--especially when it is rendered so faithfully and so lovingly as this, but more: this is just a great piece of music no matter who did it (or when it was done). (9.25/10)5. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 3rd Movement" (6:18) this one's a little different: harkening back to some of the more sophisticated, mathematical "thought experiments" that Dave Stewart might have had back in the 1970s. There is a feeling of aloneness, even reclusiveness to this piece--even with the participation of the ghosts of Mont Campbell and Clive Brooks (or Richard Sinclair and Robert Wyatt) playing bass and drums, respectively. Even the classical music-mirroring three-part construction harkens back to the work and style of Mont Campbell's EGG trio. Though this replicates some of the early Canterbury music that I am not as attached to as others, I do appreciate its faithful replication of the sound and spirit of one of my all-time favorite eras of music. (8.875/10)6. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 4th Movement" (11:50) more modern replication of the sounds and spirit of the uniquely "Canterbury" style geniuses of the 1970s composed, performed, and rendered with truly loving detail. The organ chordplay in the movement's opening minute so remind me of the genius mathematical musings of the great Dave Stewart that I almost tear up. After the 90-second intro enter piano, drums, bass, and electric guitar, gearing up into a real rip-roarer of woven tongues of flame. In the fourth minute the quartet takes a sharp turn down one of the country roads as if on a long descent from the high ground down toward the sea and its beaches and waves--where everything smooths out and soothes the soul. Here Tom chooses to introduce the lead guitar: and lo! and behold! It's Mike Oldfield (or, at least, the ghost-spirit of). I love the infusion in this piece of riffs and stylings from other realms of 1970s prog: Mike Oldfield's guitar in the sixth and seventh minutes, Tony Banks' electric piano sound and stylings, even some sound and chord play that is a nod to Jean-Luc Ponty (in the eighth minute). There is definitely genius (as well as infinite reverence) in this man's compulsion to create (and re-create) music of the artists and magical eras gone by. I find it hard to find fault with this amazing rendering. It even ends with the sound of the tolling of the church bells of some ancient gothic church as if to re-affirm the timeless and universal place that these musics have in our lives. (23/25)Total time: 45:51A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of lovingly-replicated Canterbury Style music. If you love the era, the unique sound and style of those mythical Rainbow artists, you will find yourself melting to the music on this album. Highly recommended.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Milanese impressionistic prog/J-R Fusion band continues to grow and expand--this time in even more unpredictable directions! 1. "Oort Cloud" (6:21) etheric/ambient atmospherics open this one--a long, slow development as Fender Rhodes, heavily-distorted guitar, heavy bass notes and chords, and synthesized "bassoons," "flutes," and other atmospheric noises slowly populate and fill the sound scape. Amazing that this flute is not real (or else it would be credited, right?) Nice diversion but not quite what I was expecting and/or hoping for from this band's third album. (8.667/10)2. "Vogon" (4:51) smooth Jazz-Rock Fusion that is more in the realm of what I was expecting--add the bonus of an appearance of the great theatric cabaret Jazz artist Claudio Milano to sing/recite in his Demetrio Stratos way the lyrics to a made up language that the Aether gang created themselves (inspired by Douglas Adams' Hitchiker's Guide to the Universe). I love the music! It's quite like that of one of my favorite 21st Century bands, UNAKA PRONG, from North Carolina. Much more sophisticated than the gentle/soothing-yet-dominant Fender Rhodes would reveal. Very happy-go-lucky and up-lifting. (9.25/10)3. "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres" (8:42) ambient electric guitar picking in a sonicsphere of lush reverb is thickened by the joinder of layers of keys and bass before orchestral drums and electronic keyboard and lead guitar enter to jazzify the music as if Andy Summers and Robert Fripp were together again playing with an electronica keyboard wiz. In the fifth minute things quite down as Andrea Ferrari's guitar work begins to lead the band into a kind of SONAR-scape of Minimalist Math Rock. At 5:20 then we move into a more spacious scape in which Matteo's tom-tom pattern provides the foundational movement for a jazzy Fender Rhodes solo and, later, a weave with Andrea Grumelli's heavily-treated bass and Ferrari's distorted lead guitar in the mix. The heavily-reverbed song ends with the instruments slowly dismantling and slowing down the weave, reminding me a lot of 4 AD's 1980s instrumental band DIF JUZ. Nice piece. (18/20)4. "La Mélancolie Du Petit Prince" (4:37) over/within Andrea Serino's classical piano ruminations the other instrumentalists add their tracks of untreated fretless bass, computer glitch sounds, and natural and unnatural percussion sounds. It's as if Eric Satie was caught in a sombre-yet-romantic mood playing a piano in an empty French chateau while a group of construction workers and electricians were doing restoration work in and just outside other parts of the piano's salon or grand ballroom. (I can't stop picturing Chantilly.) Or one could compare this to Ruyichi Sakamoto's 21st Century (or life-long) fascination with sound recording glitches--the work he did with Christian Fennesz and/or Alva Noto. Pretty and suitably dystopian for our times. (9/10)5. "Panta Rei" (8:00) more (a different kind of) piano-founded sound exploration: it's not always harmonically pleasing, always on the edge of being melodic in familiar Western ways, on the edge of being satisfying while never really hitting the "right" notes. It's reminiscent of 1970s exploratory jazz (think Keith Jarrett) and also Smooth Jazz (Ahmad Jamal) yet also totally pleasing--at least, until the fifth minute when Serino and Grumelli lock into a five-note, three-chord progression to support Ferrari's rock-jazz guitar solo (that reminds me of John Abercrombie, Sonny Sharrock, Larry Coryell, and Fred Frith channeling their most aggressive Jimi Hendrix and Ornette Coleman energies). The song ends with Serino's piano, all alone, gently tucking us into bed. Interesting--to say the least. I really like a lot of it, though I've never been a serious fan of the free and loose distorted guitar shredding that Ferrari uses here. (13.5/15)6. "Swerve" (10:42) thought this song opens with simple, straightforward (almost child-like) Fender Rhodes play, other tracks of synthesizer and guitars soon join in, taking the music into more serious realms. Soon Ferrari seems to be relying predominantly on a heavily-treated (reverb) guitar sound--one that reminds me of Eef Albers on Focus Con Proby's "Wingless" and "Orion" as well as the "infinity" guitars of Michael Brook and Dif Juz. By the end of the fourth minute the song has become a serious Rock-infused Jazz of the 1970s variety, even incorporating time signature slow downs and speed ups, swaying shifts into more stereotypic Rock stylistics while and before re-incorporating more Jazz-expressive sounds, lines, and motifs. Matteo Ravelli's excellent drumming plays hugely throughout this one as does Ferrari's lead guitar while Grumelli and Serino's work provides more of the foundational work to keep this one on the rails. The final motif (presented in slow down mode) sees the blending and turn-taking of all four instruments before Ferrari's last notes sound, decay, and slowly fade away. (18/20)Total Time 43:13As a blend of old and new this album stands out as an excellent bridge--one that feels experimental and exploratory while, as alluded to, also firmly expressive, even honorific, of old "classics." This alone makes it a remarkable album but also the fact of the use of totally fresh and original compositions to do so makes it doubly so. Though it's hard for me to say that I like or love this music, I do find it fascinating and I do, very much, appreciate the labor and creativity that went into creating it. This has been a fun and enjoyable album to take my time getting to know but I don't know how much I'll be listening to it once the year passes. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of genre- and stylistic-blending Jazz Fusion. The band continues to explore and progress and I commend them and urge them to continue doing so.

items.body: “En La Mar”, one of the best loved songs in the Ladino repertoire and one that also travels under the name “La Sirena”, strands a maiden alone in a tower above the sea, calling to the sailors going past, wanting love and wanting out. Rachel Valfer sings her in the Judeo-Spanish that Sephardic Jews took with them when Spain expelled them in 1492 and the Ottoman Empire gave them shelter. David Mac Lean‘s flamenco guitar brings Andalusia back to the song, and the players around it mark where the song went instead: Dan Cantrell on accordion, Faisal Zedan on Arabic percussion, Eliyahu Sills on upright bass and on the bansuri he has played with the group since their first album in 2009. The track comes from Entre Las Huertas, released on 28 August, the third album by the Bay Area’s Qadim Ensemble and the first given over entirely to Ladino. Most of it comes from the kantigas, the songs Sephardic women kept and handed on, so the record runs through lullabies, a wedding party number and a mother unloading about her straying husband while she rocks the baby to sleep. Valfer and Sills have run the group from Berkeley for close to twenty years, she singing in seven languages after six years studying maqam and Persian dastgah in Israel and Palestine, he moving between ney, oud and bass. For this album they went into the studio and played, cutting most of the record live before guests came in with flamenco guitar and qanun. Stream “En La Mar” HERE and take home Entre Las Huertas through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: The Qadim Ensemble x Rachel Valfer x Eliyahu Sills – En La Mar appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Spanish producer Nightcrawler releases the single “Reactor 4” on September 17, 2026, the first track from his forthcoming album “Uranium 235” on Nightcrawler Music. An official video accompanies the release. “Reactor 4” mixes dark techno, industrial electronics and cinematic textures. The single and its video take their titles from nuclear engineering, and Nightcrawler describes the video as the first look into the album’s dystopian universe, setting up “Uranium 235” as a concept record built around that imagery. The track was produced, mixed and mastered at NC Sound Studio, Nightcrawler’s own studio. Nightcrawler also directed the video, and cover design comes from George Gold Design, which also created the artwork for the 2025 Nightcrawler and Spammerheads collaboration “Ghostless”. “Reactor 4” arrives on all digital platforms and Bandcamp from September 17. About Nightcrawler Nightcrawler is a Spanish electronic music project active since 2011, built around horror and sci-fi film scores and a mix of dark atmospheres with driving electronic rhythms. The project released the “Strange Shadows” EP in 2014 and built out an extensive Bandcamp catalogue since, including releases such as “Visionary”, “Metropolis” and the “Corrupted System” and “R.U.S.H.” singles. In April 2025, Nightcrawler teamed up with the Valencia-based EBM duo Spammerheads for the collaborative single “Ghostless”, which Side-Line covered at the time. On November 13, 2025, Nightcrawler released the album “Malevolent Forces” through Nightcrawler Music, an eight-track record built on film-inspired EBM and spoken-word samples that Side-Line reviewed. “Reactor 4”, out September 17, 2026, is the first single from the project’s next album, “Uranium 235”. Nightcrawler continues to release music independently through Nightcrawler Music.
